title: Your practice so far

segments.voice: Yesterday, what doesn't fit, and a borrowed book handed back with thanks. Your line was not for me. Did you set something down kindly? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-four.

One question, quick to ask and harder than it sounds. Not what practice do you admire. Not what you plan to start on Monday. What did you actually do yesterday that you'd call practice? A breath before a meal. A line you said under your breath. A slow walk. A pause before a sharp reply. This path has handed you pieces for four years, and this year alone brought Tao Te Ching chapters, Montaigne's attempts, Thoreau's woods, a tour of the world's schools. Some pieces stuck. Some went back in the box. Today is an inventory, and it has one rule. Only what you actually do.
screen: `WHAT DID YOU ACTUALLY DO?` → `FOUR YEARS OF PIECES.` → `ONE RULE: ONLY WHAT YOU DO.`

segments.voice: First, admired is not the same as done. A shelf can hold books you meant to read, and a mind can hold practices you meant to keep. That's not a failing. It's just not the list we're making today. The admired list is a wish. The done list is a map, and you can only start a trip from where you really are. Second, an old check. This year we met Zengzi, a student of Confucius, who in the Analects examines himself every day on three points. Had he been loyal in working for others? Had he been trustworthy with friends? And the third: had he practiced what he was taught? Not learned. Practiced. The Analects puts the weight on doing. Third, small counts. In the book of Zechariah, in a passage about a building just begun, the prophet asks: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" A practice that has become habit can be so quiet you forget to list it. The breath before you answer. The cup of tea drunk slowly on purpose. The walk you take without your phone. Those belong on the list. Fourth, a short list is an honest list. If what you actually do fits on one line, that line is worth more than a page of plans. It's real, it's yours, and it already works in your life. Tomorrow we'll look ahead. Today, only the ground under your feet.
screen: `ADMIRED IS NOT THE SAME AS DONE.` · `ZENGZI: DID I PRACTICE IT?` · `SMALL COUNTS.` · `A SHORT LIST IS AN HONEST LIST.` · then, large: `WHAT I DO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list what you actually do. Settle, and breathe. Walk back through yesterday slowly, from waking to sleep, like rewinding a film. Each time you meet something you'd call practice, a pause, a prayer, a walk, a kind word said on purpose, note it and keep going. Don't add the things you meant to do. If the list is short, let it be short. If you pray, put prayer on the list exactly as it really happens. The bell holds the time. When it rings, write the list down.
Your practice so far. Not the practices you admire, but the ones you actually do, gathered from four years of pieces. Today's word.
Your line: what I do. Today, pick one thing from your list and do it on purpose, noticing it while you do it, the way Zengzi asked whether he'd practiced. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: People who keep a personal spiritual practice often take stock at the end of a season by writing down what they actually do each day and week, rather than what they hope to do, and build from that list.

original.note: Chinese xi, to practice or rehearse: the word in Zengzi's third check (Analects 1.4).

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of every practice you've heard of this year.
what it means: only what you actually do, small things included, because a real map starts where you are.
what a scholar hears: Zengzi's check in Analects 1.4, which asks not whether he learned but whether he practiced.
